It may also be that the hon. member has concealed his talents expecting to take the world by surprise at some time or another, but up to the present time, judging by the footprints on the sands of his political life I daresay that the Dominion of Canada will look upon him as more closely related to the prehistoric tribe to which he implied that I belonged more than any other man.
Would my hon. friend allow me? If he attaches that interpretation to what I said, in answer to a question from him, he is altogether wrong.
I most decidedly took that interpretation. I had made up my mind not to lower myself by replying, but the longer I sat down the more piqued I felt, and you now have my resentment to your remark.
If the hon. gentleman will allow me? I never attached that meaning to my remark; I said that only to show what was done in the past, if it was wrong, could be remedied in the present.
I accept my hon. friend's apology.
It is not an apology; it is an explanation.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I shall continue the even course of my speech without paying any regard to the - hon. member's explanation, because it is too lame even to stand by itself.
Now, Sir, I do agree with a number of the remarks made by gentlemen on the Opposition side, because I have had the good fortune of living in the province of Quebec and know what transpires there in a large measure; but hon. gentlemen from that province have not had the good fortune of living out West, and when they seek to set for us a standard which obtains in their province, they should at least be.acquainted with the conditions which obtain in our western country.
In the province of Quebec the prothono-tary is, nine times out of ten, a man chosen from the legal profession, a man who as a matter of fact has the recommendation in some form or other of his profession. Incidentally he may have been a politician to

a certain extent, but he is looked upon as a gentleman who by reason of his standing in the profession is capable of discharging that office with dignity and satisfaction. The registrar in the province of Quebec is usually a lawyer, or some person of high standing in the community, who by reason of his political life or otherwise is given that position, and usually he discharges that office with a great deal of fairness. I can cite the committee an instance in Compton county where the registrar was Mr. Orr, a very fine gentleman indeed, and my father was the deputy registrar. Notwithstanding that they both discharged their duties very fairly at election times, the Liberal Government of the province saw to it that a man by the name of Willian Leonard from Sherbrooke was appointed instead of my father, who was then an old gentleman and had not at any time taken part in politics. However, I find no fault with that; it was the patronage system, and it is the patronage system still in that province.
The municipalities in the province of Quebec are governed in an entirely different way to the municipalities in our western provinces. In the former province we have well defined municipal boundaries and a population which is homogeneous and crystallized. We have no such thing in Western Canada.
I can see the fairness of the remarks made by hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec, because I know the system under which they operate in that province. But what have we got out West? I will take the province of Alberta first. No man appointed by the Provincial Government except the Clerk of the Supreme Court has the sanction of any person or body. That man as a rule, apart from being a politician, is a barrister, and the Bar Association usually give the Government its advice upon the appointment. Every other office is held by a political heeler. In my election, I had as organizer a man by the name of Wadleigh, who was formerly organizer for Frank Oliver-I had confidence in that man because I knew he was favourable to the politics of my party. He organized for one provincial constituency, Beaver River. What did he find? He found that the principal Land Title men were opposing him in his organization-that the registrars of the Land Titles offices permitted their employees to go out and work against him. As a matter of fact they emptied the court house in the city of Edmonton so far as they could dispense with the services of their officials for the time being and placed them in the city to oppose me. Every department of the Provincial Government was ransacked and all the officials, outside of the deputy ministers and the other departmental heads, were placed in my constituency to work against me. Those men had to perform these duties because the chiefs in every one of those departments told them they had to go and do that work. We do not find this system prevailing in Quebec. By reason of the experience and stability of that province we find men in office who can be trusted. But if you were to appoint the sheriff of my district as my returning officer, he would make a call on Charlie Cross to give him the balance of the organization against me, and Charlie's motto is: "I fly the black flag, so look out for yourselves." Before you appoint that man to conduct my election, I say that I am just as capable of finding a good partisan as you can find.
Now, Sir, if I thought my hon. friends on the opposite side were sincere, and were not merely to-day repeating the same political expedients that during the whole course of their political career they have favoured,
I might be more inclined to listen to them. When I find the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gannon) and others so far removed from their prehistoric ancestors that they can teach others how to conduct themselves in politics and otherwise, I wish they would first of all start lecturing those Liberals in the western provinces on how to conduct themselves when they are holding elections.
It is said that a returning officer has
great powers; yes, he has. But the powers that are given to a returning officer in Alberta are as follows:
If the enumerator in like manner is fully satisfied that there is on the list the name of any person who is not qualified as a voter in such polling subdivision he may draw erasing lines through such name and write his own initials opposite thereto in the column for remarks.
Which means that during the few days before the polling the enumerator gives notice of a place where he is to be found and people may come to him and say, 'You have left off the list so many people, and they are entitled to vote." He will place those names on the list. But in another section of the Alberta Election Act that same enumerator may immediately after that, if he is satisfied, pass his pencil through those names and turn over to the deputy returning officer the morning of the poll an entirely different list than the one prepared by the enumerator.

So that when a man does come to vote, he. is challenged under our provincial Act, He has to swear his vote. His 'ballot is enclosed in an envelope. There has been a number of polls in a riding where the ballot boxes contained nothing but sealed envelopes. What have the voters to do in order to count their votes? They must appear before a justice of the peace, who notifies them that he will sit at a certain time in a certain place for the purpose of counting these votes. When the voters get there they find that the justice of the peace has moved to another place and subsequently all get a second notice informing them that the justice of the peace will sit not at place number one, but at place number two. Of course it is too late, and then the whole poll is lost. Let the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) teach the Liberals of that Government how to conduct themselves. Let hon. gentlemen opposite teach morality and decency among themselves before they tell us that we should conduct ourselves better than we have conducted ourselves in the past.
It seems to me that if we go back to the election of 1911 we can hardly be told by hon. members opposite that we are going back to the time before the deluge. In 1911, when they had the running of the election, their morality was dormant. It has been kindled and awakened only within a very short time indeed, because at that time in Ontario they named as returning officers sheriffs or registrars in only twelve or thirteen constituencies out of eighty-six. West of the Great Lakes they did not name any sheriffs or registrars as returning officers. If you refer to the sessional papers of 1912, pages 10 and 11 and following pages, you will find that my statement is true. It is indeed marvellous, Sir, that we should have a new birth so suddenly. I am afraid that the three stages of labour have been omitted in this birth. I am inclined to believe that the professions which these gentlemen make are like all professions which they have made to the country; at first they deceive the public, and at last they betray it.
The member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) has said that the Tory party was a party of the class. Well, I think we have attended the funeral of the Tory party. I suggest that if my hon. friend consults the member for Dorchester' he will be advised that he should not refer to those things because they are of the past. We are advanced; we are wearing clothes, whereas the Tory party was probably naked, to use the con-
struction of my hon. friend from Dorchester. I believe that the Tory party has been buried; we are dealing entirely with new conditions and a new party. If the Tory party were a class, at least they advocated only one sort of thing and carried out only one sort of thing. They were consistent; they did not go before the public as my hon. friends opposite have done and tell them what they would do for them when they got into power, and then absolutely adhere to the poor, despised Tory party politics.
The hon. member for Joliette did make a suggestion which has some merit: that the Civil Service Commission should make these appointments. I am just as anxious as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's that we should have clean elections ; that our elections should be conducted by men who are absolutely non-partisan. But to the best of my ability I will oppose the adoption of any amendment which has the effect of substituting one class of partisans for another. The Civil Service Commission is on trial. It has been carrying on only for a short time. I shall have occasion to complain about the Civil Service Commission as regards appointments which they have made in my riding; it is my privilege to do so under the Civil Service Act. Just how far the Civil Service Commission could be of assistance to us under this Act I am not certain; the hon. member for Joliette did not satisfy me fully that the commission could completely undertake this work. If my recollection is correct, there is a provision in the Civil Service Act that the commission shall obtain advice regarding appointments from the deputy heads of the various departments here and, in the provinces and particularly in rural constituencies, shall consult postmasters or other officials of the Government. Well, if the advice given by the deputy heads and by postmasters in rural districts would be no better under this Act than that which has been given in connection with some of the appointments that have been made, I am afraid that the suggestion of the hon. member for Joliette will not be very satisfactory to any of us. However, if I can be convinced by my hon. friend from Joliette and his friends that the 'Civil Service Commission, being largely removed from politics, can do greater service to the country in this regard than we ourselves can do, then I shall be ready to support his view. Until that time I shall support the law as it is, because anything that has so far been sug-

gested is merely lor the purpose of assisting the Opposition into power. And let me say this: if we had adopted the amendment which was voted down and hon. gentlemen opposite came into power-though I doubt that, they ever shall-they would be the first ones to amend that legislation by saying that upon trial it did not work out satisfactorily.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at Eight o clock, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
iMr LAPOINTE:	I do not purpose doing
as my hon. friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie) who preceded me did, and discuss over again the amendment which has been disposed of by the committee. The argument set forth by my hon. friend showed that we were right in the stand which we were taking on this clause. He invited us to go to Alberta and reform the conditions that existed there, and he said that they are the very conditions which will prevail under this legislation as it stands. He quoted facts and brought forward arguments to show, and prove, that the system in Alberta is wrong. It is not for us to reform Alberta; it is for the people of Alberta to do that; but we do not want their methods to prevail in Dominion elections, and that is why we oppose the clause as it now reads.
The amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) has been disposed of, and I would suggest another way of dealing with the clause. The Chief Electoral Officer will be a permanent official. We are giving him great powers; his functions will be almost judicial functions; he will be independent of the Government and oif political parties. Why not give him jurisdiction in the appointment of returning officers?
Mr. PETER iMcGIBBON (Muskoka): What would the Chief Electoral Officer know about conditions, say in Vancouver?

What does the Governor General in Council know about returning officers in the various ridings? The Governor General in Council in this case means the minister representing the particular province. In my province the minister would be the hon. gentleman who is supposed to represent it in the Senate. He is going to appoint returning officers in my riding and in the constituencies of the hon. gentlemen from that province. What does he. know about the returning officers in the various constituencies? He gets information from the sitting member or the defeated candidate, as the case may be, or the chiefs of his party in the particular constituency. There is nothing to prevent the Chief Electoral Officer, who will be, or who at any rate, is supposed to be, an independent party, from getting the same information. He will get information from my hon. friend as regards his constituency; he may get information from me as regards my constituency, but he may get information from somebody else also. He may consult authorities in the various constituencies and, as his functions will Ire of a permanent character, he will be able to do that prior to election time. He may first inquire as to who would be the best man to be a returning officer in a constituency, then get into communication with that man and educate him as to his duties when the election takes place, and thus avoid many of the difficulties, delays and troubles that happen at every election.
He is a permanent official.

Yes. I offer the suggestion to the Acting tSolicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) who has invited us to make suggestions, and I really think that this 'question is a serious one and that we are not wasting the time of the committee in discussing it as was suggested this afternoon. The question of fairness and unfairness arises at election times. However fair a cause may be, that cause cannot succeed against crookedness and unfair methods. We want 'fairness in elections, we want electoral machinery that will do justice to everybody; and I think this suggestion of mine would go far to relieve what is in the public mind as to what may happen under the system which will be established under the present legislation.

speechtext:
Since the amendment
to this clause was voted on, two suggestions have been made. One is that returning officers should be appointed by the Civil Service Commission, a commission that has jurisdiction over the appointment of the Civil 'Service of this country, and which is thoroughly-

If the minister will allow
me, I will withdraw my suggestion, and will support the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe), because his suggestion is much better than mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the
suggestion that the Civil Service 'Commission should have authority to make the

appointments of returning officers has been withdrawn.
Mr. DENI'S: So far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought when it was
made that it was rather hollow. The suggestion, however, which has now been made by my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) is one that has received considerable attention from the Government.' The question of appointing permanent officials was one that was thoroughly considered;, likewise our best consideration was given to the question of appointments by the Chief Electoral Officer, and after the best consideration we could give to every method, we decided that the old system was preferable to any other. The office of Chief Electoral Officer is a position created for the first time under this Bill. His knowledge of conditions in Canada is necessarily limited. The first suggestion arose from that individual himself, and he intimated in plain language that it would foe impossible for him to select returning officers. He said that he would have to rely on information supplied to him from other sources, his suggestion being that it would come from the members. But to my mind, there is a greater objection than that. We have appointed him a permanent official; we have clothed him with almost, judicial powers; we have placed his office on the same plane as that of judges, and (he cannot be removed except for cause. If he had the appointment of returning officers in this country, no matter how honest his intention might he, somewhere or another in Canada there might he a slip-there have been, slips in the past-and that high functionary, the Chief Electoral Officer, would immediately be charged with partisanship. The same result would happen in the, case of a judge, if a judge were given the appointment of these returning officers. There is no system ever devised in this country or any other country, so far as I know, which could be called a perfect system. We have to take into account the fact that there might be some mishap, some misadventure, some bad appointment. That will not be the rule, but probably the rare exception, and if such a thing takes place, where ;s the responsibility? Under the clause as it stands, the responsibility rests upon the Government, The responsibility must rest upon some one's shoulders.
But there is another point and one worthy of some consideration, It is enacted by section 42 of the British NoTtb America Act, which gives this Parliament its constitution, that the Governor General |Mr. Guthrie.]
is the person who shall assemble and dissolve Parliament, and issue writs, and the like: and the old statute of this House has always been that the Governor General shall make these appointments. Whether or not the present proposal is an infringement upon the Royal prerogative, I will not say, but I think in the light of present constitutional methods, When we speak oi power being given to the Governor General, we mean the Governor General advised by hlis council, and i*n the present Bill, the language has been changed from that of the British North America Act and it has been placed in .the present clause as the Governor General in Council. Constitutionally, and under the strict letter of the law, it may be that we should have left out the words "in Council," but I fancy that His Excellency the Governor General would never undertake to issue a writ unless advised by his council that he Should do so. At this distance of time, after the experience of centuries under our British system, I think we all agree that His Excellency the Governor General in this country and His Majesty, the King, in Great Britain, act, in such cases, only on the advice of their ministers. We have S0' stated in this Bill, and I doubt very much if, under the language of our constitutional Act, it would be permmissible for us to allow the King's writ o.r, in this case, His Excellency's writ, to issue except in the method prescribed by the constitutional Act-. There is not only the question of the appointment, but the tetill greater question of the responsibility. The responsibility in the present instance rests upon the Government. If the Government does wrong, if bad appointments are made, the people have their remedy in Parliament. That is not so in the case of appointments by the Chief Electoral Officer.
But I can see practical reasons why the system proposed in the Bill is better than the system proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe). I believe we shall have better returning officers under the present Bill than we should have under the system which he suggests, and my reason for stating so is the candid confession of the Parliamentary Counsel himself, who says thaf he would be in absolute ignorance as to conditions in the various ridings of Canada and would have to be guided by the advice of somebody, and those somebodies would likely be the members of this House. In the one case you have the authority of the Governor General in Council for the appointment, and you have likewise the responsibility upon the Government; in

the other case you have the limited knowledge and the irresponsibility. For my part I must say that, as between the two systems, I very imuch prefer the system we have operated under ever since we had a country here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 28-polling divisions: -
I ask that this section be allowed to stand. The leader of the Opposition is not here and I believe he has some remarks to make in reference to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection.
Section stands.
On section 29-Qualifications of electors:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that this section stand. Some hon. members on the other side have requested that sections 29 and 32 be not proceeded with before Tuesday, and I have agreed to that proposal.
Section stands.
On section 30-Disqualification of electors:
In the last line on page 12, subclause (a), the words "Governor in Council" are used. I think this should read "Governor General in Council."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is right. I move
that the subclause be amended by adding after the word " Governor" in line 38 the word "General."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.	.

In subsection (2) any person who votes, or induces or procures any other person to vote at an election, knowing that such person is for any reason disqualified, or is non-qualified or incompetent to vote, shall be guilty of an illegal practice. Why not include persons who have been already condemned for such practices?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is not necessary because a man can be sworn at the polls as to whether he has eyer committed an illegal practice, and if he has he can be deprived of his vote. There is another Act on the statute book applying to corrupt and illegal practices and^ the punishment meted out to wrong-doers. Under that there is no condemnation until after trial, but there has always been in our oath a clause to prohibit from voting men who have been guilty of bribery and corruption. It has not been' very effective, but that has always been the law.

What is meant by the disfranchisement referred to in subclause
(O?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is the same clause as the one under the former law. The Disfranchising Act has been on the statute book for many years and it applies to persons guilty of corrupt practices. It provides a mode of investigation and trial, and the penalty is one of seven years disqualification as well as other penalties imposed by the Act.

Subclause (g) provides that persons who by the laws of any province are disqualified from voting for a member of the legislative assembly of such province in respect of race shall not be qualified to vote in that province under this Act. The clause goes on to say:
Provided, however, that the provisions of this paragraph shall not disqualify or render incompetent to vote any person who has served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada in the late war-.
Should you not add after "Canada" the words "Great Britain and the Allies"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That would open a pretty wide subject, and I do not know that I would be favourable to the suggestion. Such persons as that proposal would include might not be British subjects.
Mr. POWErt: That objection is fully met in section 29 which emphatically declares that they must he British subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
When we come to that
section the whole question will be open for discussion.

If we got through with section 30 to-night we might not be able to return to this particular paragraph on another occasion, and it strikes me that we should allow Imperial soldiers who fought, if they are otherwise duly qualified, to vote. There is no reason why we should not.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If we included every one wdio fought in the late war for Great Britain and the Allies-

Well, leave out the Allies.
Mr. CrUTHRIE:	Those persons have not
the qualifications upon which we insist in section 29.
Certain British subjects who are otherwise fully qualified under section 29 might be disqualified under subclause (g) of section 30.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is only where they are disqualified by a provincial law.

Certain British subjects
who fought for Great Britain during the late war and who are otherwise fully qualified to vote might be disqualified by the legislature of some province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Hardly.
Well, if they would not be disqualified why not allow soldiers who fought for Great Britain and her Allies to come under the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The clause in this section is intended to protect those who by reason of race may be disqualified through any provincial law. If they fought in the Canadian naval or military forces they will be protected ip their vote. I cannot imagine that any provincial law disqualifies any British or French subject.
. Mr. POWER': What about Hindus?
Mr. GUTHRIE;: The Act does apply to Hindus.

If Hindus generally are excluded from the franchise, at least those Hindus who fought in France and throughout the world on behalf of Great Britain and the Allies should be considered. You are giving the vote to Hindus who fought in the Canadian army-I presume there were some who, did-and I do not see any reason why the Hindu in the British army should be discriminated against. If you exclude one you should exclude the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We do not make an exception of any one. We merely recognize the provincial disqualification imposed by the law of any province by reason of race.

You say, however, that if a man who is disqualified by race has fought in the naval or military forces of Canada he will be permitted to vote in spite of that provincial disqualification. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Then, why not give the privilege to men of the same race who fought in the Imperial forces?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that there would be many cases of this character. There might be an isolated case here and there, but I do not think we should change the whole law merely to meet one or two exceptions. So far as I have had evidence on the subject-and I have got it from 
official	sources-there were about 194
Japanese who were British subjects and who enlisted in the forces of Canada. Over fifty of them lost their lives in the campaign, forty came home badly wounded, and the rest returned whole in body and mind. There were also a few British subjects of Chinese origin, but I believe the number was very' limited-something like twelve. I have been informed that there were no men in British Columbia of Hindu origin who fought in the forces of Canada. Subsection (g) will have very limited application in any event.

Were any of the Hindus
in British Columbia British subjects or British reservists?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have heard there were only two. I do not know whether there were any reservists or not.

Would it not be possible
that we should at some future time invite to this country British or Hindu reservists?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We can amend the law if we decide to do so.
I object to any disqualification against any British soldier-being put upon the statutes of Canada. If they are good enough to fight they were good enough to vote. ,

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to subsection (f). This subsection specifies three classes of persons who will not have the right to vote. These are (1) prisoners undergoing punishment for criminal offences; (2) persons in lunatic asylums, and (3) persons
-who are maintained in whote or in part as inmates receiving charitable support or care in municipal poorhouses or houses of industry, or are inmates receiving charitable support in any institution receiving aid from the government of a province under any statute in that behalf.
1 wish to direct the attention of the minister to the third class. This is a condition which exists in the city from which I comq. We have charitable institutions which receive inmates. Some of these inamtes pay partly for their keep; others do not pay at all. I submit that those who pay a certain amount for their keep, say $10 a month, should have the right to vote. These people are only maintained by charity to a certain extent. The clause which I have just quoted provides that inmates of a charitable institution which receives aid from the government of a province under a statute in that behalf has no right to vote. In my city we have a charitable institution which

has, we will say, 100 inmates and it receives from the province of Quebec between $200 and $400 a year.
For each patient?

Not for each patient but
for the whole institution. The expense of keeping these inmates runs into thousands of dollars. It just happens that the provincial government distributes a very small budget each year amongst charitable institutions. This clause, read strictly according to the letter, provides that the inmates of all these institutions which receive however small an amount from the province shall be deprived of their votes. Probably these conditions are not known to the minister and I would like to call them to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Unless there were very grave reasons I would not change this clause. It was put in the law many years, ago deliberately, and it is based upon the principle that a man who is receiving public charity is for that period of time disfranchised.

If a man receives public
charity in part only, if his board is worth $40 or $50 a month and he pays half of that amount and receives charity for the balance, is it right that he should be deprived of his vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He is disqualified under this section. He is really an inmate of a charitable institution.

That is not right at
all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It was considered right for a number of years.

These institutions are only receiving $400 a year from the Quebec Government. What good reason can you give for depriving a man under these circumstances of his vote? It is not because men are poor that they cannot judge of what is going on in this country and it is not because they are poor that they should not be allowed to vote. My hon. friend (Mr. Denis is absolutely right when he says that in these institutions in the small cities in Quebec there are people who are paying for half of their board. The Government pay only $400 a year as aid to an institution of this kind, and I do not see why these poor people should be deprived of their votes.

Would the
hon. gentleman extend that privilege to the inmates of poorhouses, Indians and wards of the Government?

Even although a man be poor in this country he should not be deprived of his vote.
Mr. G.UTHRIE: A man's poverty is not the test. The poorest man in Canada can vote, but if he is receiving Government aid, or is a ward of the Government, he should not vote.

Do you call $400 a
year for the maintenance of 100 inmates in an institution, Government aid?
Yes, I do.
Well you ought to be ashamed of it.

I would like to ask the
minister if he would not kindly accept as a friendly suggestion that he strike out in line 14 the words " or in part." I do not think it would hurt anybody to give the vote to a man who has a revenue of $300 a year but whose income is not sufficient to pay for his board entirely. A portion of his board is paid, not by the State, but by charitable contributions from somebody else. I believe it will be perfectly in order to allow that man to vote. He has at least half the right of a citizen as he pays for half of his board.
Give the vote to all.

I would not like to let it go on record in Hansard that persons referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Gauvreau) would be deprived of their votes. The section applies only to those " inmates receiving charitable support in any institution receiving aid from the Government of a province under any statute in that behalf." These institutions that my hon. friend has referred to are getting $400, as he says, but not under statute. These are subventions or subsidies that are granted each year by the Government.
The subsidy is a statute.

I do not think there
are statutory subventions every year. I would like the minister's opinion on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I prefer the section as it is drawn. A government that was evil disposed could line up a grand squad of voters by simply boarding a public institution of this country. That is not permitted under this clause. There is a good reason for this provision. It was charged at one time in the province of Ontario that institutions in the city of Hamilton were used by the Ontario Government as nothing but hives for parties who voted

at election times, until that was stopped by law. Anybody who receives public aid should not be entitled to exercise the franchise while receiving that aid.
Quite right, but there are institutions, as my hon. friend (Mr. Gauvreau) has pointed out, where the people are paying the full amount, or a fair amount, for their board.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: they would not be disqualified.

Yes, because these institutions have other functions to perform and they are subsidized to a certain extent. It may be only a small amount, say $400 a year, to assist them in doing the work they have to do. Are men who are paying a fair amount for their board at such an institution to be deprived of their vote, just because the institution is receiving a few hundred dollars from the Provincial Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, a man who is paying a fair amount for his board is not deprived of his vote; there is no question about that. But if his board is paid for in whole or in part by the institution he is deprived of his vote. I know several institutions that charge what my hon. friend calls a fair amount. These boarders are not charity patients; they pay their way.
But if the institution receives a small amount of assistance from the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That does not disqualify them.
The law does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The section reads:
Persons who	are maintained in whole
or in part as inmates receiving charitable support or care in municipal poorhouses or houses of industry, or are inmates receiving charitable support in any institution receiving aid from the government of a province under any statute in that behalf.
It says " inmates receiving charitable support." If they pay their way, or pay a fair amount as my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) has suggested, I have no hesitation in saying, they are not disqualified.

Let me give an
illustration. In the province of Quebec farmers may he left in their old age with no children to take further care of, and they may have a couple of thousand dollars saved up. They go to a charitable institution and say:	Will you keep us for the

balance of our lives if we give you this $2,000? The institution accepts it. Under this section those men would be deprived of their votes because they were in an institution receiving aid from a Provincial Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I say, no; but if they
were in what is popularly know as a poor-house, or a house of industry, they would not be entitled to vote under this section.
That is what we complain of.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision is old,
and I think it is founded in good sense.

A man may not cost the institution anything, but still may be receiving " charitable support." Suppose I put a poor man in an institution subsidized by the Provincial Government. I pay for his board. Therefore, he is receiving charitable support from me in an institution subsidized by the Government. He would not be entitled to vote under this section.

Do you think he
should have a vote?

Why not, if I think he is honest and decent enough for me to deprive myself of $20 or $25 a month to see him taken care of, I think he deserves the vote just as much as anybody else. Some men have money and don't deserve votes, and others have no money and you are depriving them of votes. You ought not to value a man or citizenship by the dollar stam dard, but that seems to have been the standard followed in too much legislation recently. The dollar seems to have been almighty. That is not the principle we stand for on this side of the House. It is not the man who carries his soul in his purse that makes a good citizen, but the man with a soul and a heart. I think a man without a dollar who is good enough to be taken care of by his fellow-citizens in a charitable institution should have the vote just as much as myself or thq hon. member (Mr. Griesbach).
I think the clause is susceptible of another interpretation. It says "receiving charitable support in any institution receiving aid from the Government." Now the charitable support may come from some source outside of the institution, but under this section the man would be disqualified because he was receiving such support while in any institution subsidized 'by the Government.

The general proposition in a free state is that the franchise shall be exercised by free and independent electors, and in my judgment it is most important that we should so provide. A man who lives by charity is neither free nor independent.
Then you would deprive a son, twenty-one years of age or oveT, of the vote if he was supported by his father?
That is not charity.
He is supported by his father while attending school.

In the case cited by my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) of a person paying a fixed sum for his board, if that sum is accepted in actuarial expectation of life, it is a payment, not charity. I would fancy that the law as originally drafted was based on the assumption that in a free state the franchise could be exercised only by those who are free and independent.

In Ontario the Provincial Government gives a certain subsidy to the general hospitals. Now by too strict a reading of this clause it might be taken that the patients in these general hospitals were disqualified from voting, but as a matter of fact this clause is an old one and they never have been debarred from voting. Patients in general hospitals in this province have always voted in an election. I have seen that they have got out to vote at some elections myself. There is nothing in the law against it. I do not think the clause would apply to the institutions referred to by my hon. friend and others, or to institutions such as general hospitals. I think this clause is intended to apply specifically to poorhouses, where the inmates are absolute wards of the Government.
Why not say so in the clause?

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Mandon)is absolutely right. The clause could easily be amended to make that point clear by substituting for the words "are maintained in whole or in part as inmates receiving charitable support" the words "are maintained in whole as inmates receiving charitable support." Otherwise, if a man pays $200 for his board in such an institution it may be contended that as the board is worth $400 his contribution of $200 is really only half of his board, the remainder being "charitable support." I contend that we should amend this clause by striking out the words "or in part" and
making the clause read that a man will be disqualified to vote when he is wholly maintained as indicated, and not in part only.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is rather aimusing to me to listen to the speech of my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) and to notice the mock indignation which he affects in condemning tihis clause as constituting a property test for the exercise of the franchise. My hon. friend was a member of the government that deliberately enacted this Clause in 1896, and deliberately re-enacted it .in 1908; and in 1894 when the clause first appeared on our statute books it was passed at the instance of the Liberal Opposition, it being charged that the Government of the day could utilize these poor-houses or charitable institutions for the purpose of colonizing votes which they could lead out on election day if they saw fit. The clause was inserted at the instigation of the Liberal party; so if it constitutes a property qualification, who is to blame for it?
Is that a reason why we should not change it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is absolutely -sound in principle. There should be no property qualification or no test of riches in this country. But where a man is in the position of being a ward of the Government and is receiving public aid, I do not think he is entitled to the franchise. We have recognized that principle in our legislation in other respects, that being the way we have treated our Indian wards; they have not .a. vote yet, and they do not get it under this Bill. Any one, therefore, who is receiving money from the Government which in the final analysis is given by way of charity, should not he qualified to vote. That principle has been recognized since 1894, .and was re-affirmed twice, in 1896 and in 1908, by the Government of which my hon. friend from Three Rivers was a member. The Government to-day re-affirms that principle in the present Bill, and I think it is a very proper principle.

The hon. gentleman did not understand my point at all. I say that under this clause the fact of being an inmate of an institution .subsidized by the Government disqualifies a man, although he receives no aid.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not a line of that has been changed; it is the same word for word as the language in the old Act.

That makes no difference. My hon. friend laughs at .what he calls my mock indignation, and seems surprised that

I may have changed my mind. The Minister of Militia and Defence and Acting Solicitor General is surprised that a man changes his mind! Well, Sir, this is a climax. I have changed my mind, and for cause.
Because you are in opposition.

Because I am in opposition? No ! Because I find something lacking in the clause. I dissent from it not from personal motives; I do not care whether the inmates of any of these institutions vote or not, but they are a class that I want to protect, for I contend that an inmate who costs the institution nothing ought not to be disqualified from voting. The disqualification is not based on the amount of aid he receives from the institution, but it is based on where he happens to be at the time he receives the aid. If the clause were to read:
-as inmates receiving charitable support or care in municipal poorhouses or houses of industry, or inmates receiving charitable support in and from any institution receiving aid from the government of a province under any statute in that behalfthat would be fair. But the word "from" is not in this clause, and a man may receive Charitable support in an institution, although that support may cost the institution nothing.
Now, the fact that this principle has been enacted and re-enac'ted, I think, is no answer; any man who wishes to be serious in any argument o-ught to drop the tu quoque. There is nothing more amusing than to see my hon. friend the Acting Solicitor General coming back and crying over his past sins when he was a Liberal and reproaching Liberals for rvvhat they have done.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not reproach, 1 uphold them.

I know; bu't in other circumstances you have reproached the Liberal party and tried to get behind them in order to cover your own skin. But that will not do-. We are going to discuss the question on its merits, and my hon. friend may talk in stentorian tones and with all his accustomed dignity, but he is not going to scare me out of this discussion. Mine is not mock indignation. As I said just now, I do not belong to. the bunch who carry their, souls in their purses; I carry my heart in my breast, and I have enough sense of justice to try to protect men who deserve to be protected.

I move, Mr. Chairman, to amend clause (f) of subsection 1 of section 30 by adding after the word "support" in the sixteenth line the words "and from."

I think the whole question comes down to the interpretation to be given to the words "charitable support." In our province very often an old man will give his savings of $500 or $600 to' a charitable institution so that he may be maintained there for the rest of his life. Will such a person be disqualified under this clause? He is wholly supported by the charitable institution, but that support he gets in consideration of the amount he gave when he entered the institution. I would like to knoiw what interpretation the Acting Solicitor General would give to such a case. Would the man be disentitled to vote? If he is, I think at is very unfair. This is a very important question, Mr. Chairman. We have institutions in our province maintaining hundreds of people under the conditions that I have mentioned, but because for some reason or other the Government gives a paltry sum to that institution, arei we:	going to1 deprive
those people of their right to vote? I would be willing to accept the clause as it stands provided we had a proper interpretation of the words "charitable support," but there is no such interpretation anywhere In the Bill. Who is going to tell us what it means? Where is "charitable support" to begin and where is it to end? My hon. friend '(Mr. Bureau), with that elevation of mind which characterizes his participation 'in every debate in the House, has carried the question to a higher level and has put it to us in the following form: will a rich man be entitled to vote because he is rich and a poor man be deprived of his right to vote because he is poor? The qualification of a voter is not to be found in the dollars that he possesses but in the brains that Jie may have. When I meet some gentlemen who have inherited lots of money, I thank Heaven that 'they did so, because if they had not inherited money they would never have been able to earn five cents for themselves. If the poor man is not entitled to vote, then this is no longer a democratic country. The minister should give heed to ancient history. In many cities in Greece only poor 9 p.m. men were entitled to vote, rich men were debarred; 'because the people thought that having individual and personal interest of his own, the rich man could not consider a question on its merits as a poor man could. I think'there is much in favour of that contention.

Mr. I.APOINTE:	It will not take on
the other side.
Mr. QANtNION: I know that on the other side rich men are often heard with more interest and more consideration than poor men. When electors like Sir William Mackenzie, Sir Donald -Mann, Sir Joseph Fla-velle and Lord Atholstan cast their ballots on any question, their decision is listened to with more interest than that of the poor man who has only fifty cents in his pocket. I do my best to believe that the minister is sincere when he tells us that he wants to have a fair franchise law. If he is, ho>v can he consistently incorporate in this Bill a clause which can be so interpreted as to have the effect of withholding the vote from a man simply because he is poor?

Let us suppose that a disabled returned soldier receives from the Government a pension; that that pension is not sufficient for his support or maintenance and that he goes into some charitable institution and pays that pension to the institution on account of his board. Suppose that the amount of the pension is not sufficient to pay for his maintenance in that institution. The man may be crippled and unable to do any work. Such a man is supported partly by charity; is the minister of the opinion that he should lose his right to vote? He certainly loses it under this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has put a somewhat extreme case. I understood that our pensions were administered upon the principle that a man should receive enough to prevent his being the object or subject of charity. However, lest such a case might happen as my hon. friend has referred to, I shall be content to put a provision in this section to the effect that it shall not apply to a returned soldier.

What about the case of
a man who gives $600 to a charitable institution? Is he debarred from voting?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It depends upon whether or not he is there as a charitable patient. If he pays his way, he is not debarred from voting.
Mr.* GANNON: Who is going to decide?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose there are tribunals that decide all these questions. If the voter is subsequently prosecuted the matter would certainly be decided by the courts. The last clause provides for that.

Would the returning officer
put him on the electoral list?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is a matter which the returning officer will have to decide; I cannot decide it for him. Every case will have to rest on its own merits. To my mind, the language is clear. A charitable patient is not a person who is a subject of 'private charity; he has to be in an institution. Whether he is paying his way or not is a point of fact, and the facts, I assume, will differ in almost every case; but I would have no difficulty in deciding, if I knew the fact, whether the man was paying his way or whether he was receiving charity, and I do not think any one else would have any difficulty. I can quite understand, if a man goes to an institution and makes a bargain for his keep, based on his probability of life, even if it is speculative, that is not charity, it is a bargain; and if the man lives twice as long as was contemplated, that is not chartiy, it is a bargain.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have, I presume, at least one sanatorium in each province, and there are in the sanatoriums to-day hundreds of patients receiving treatment who are not returned soldiers. The charges in these sanatoriums are not sufficient to cover expenses, and the sanatoriums receiving grants from the Provincial Governments. Will patients such as I describe be debarred from voting under this measure? Patients in hospitals would be in the same position.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The question is whether they are receiving charity. A man who is paying his way in a hospital or a sanatorium, a man who is paying the fee prescribed by the institution, is not receiving charity.
Supposing he is a poor man?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If he is receiving charity, he is disqualified.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The charges in the sanatoriums, at least in Saskatchewan, are not sufficient to* cover expenses, and grants are made by the Provincial Government and by charitable individuals. Therefore, I contend that the inmate of such a sanatorium is receiving charity.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If a hospital or a sanatorium fixes a rate which applies to all persons as the rate at which patients shall be admitted to that institution, that is not charity; that is paying your way.

There are a number of members who are honestly dissatis-

fled with this clause as it stands, there being a fear that some people who should not be debarred from voting will be debarred. I know that, in our province at least, the hospitals and sanatoriums are receiving what might be called charitable support; they are supported partially by the Provincial Government, and the patients are not supposed to pay the full amount that is required for their keep. I am not saying that a judge would decide that they were receiving charity; I do not say that he would decide otherwise; I do not know what I would do were I a judge. But I think the minister should take a little pains to see that this clause is so clearly worded that these people will know whether they have a right to vote or not. I do_not, for a moment, want to associate myself with those who consider that people in poor-houses, or who are receiving public charity, should have a vote, because I think the Government is quite right in refusing to give the franchise to those who are practically wards of the Government.
The hon. member is wrong all the same.

I may be wrong, or I may be right; but it is quite common throughout the Dominion that inmates of hospitals and sanatoriums are receiving what might be called charitable support, and I think the minister should make it clear that those people are not covered by this clause.

I believe this is mostly a misunderstanding and the minister can easily cover it by simply adding to this clause the words "this clause shall not apply to inmates of institutions such as hospitals who pay the prescribed fees of those institutions," As regards the Toronto General Hospital or hospitals in any other Ontario city, there is a prescribed fee, such as perhaps one dollar per day to be paid by patients in what are called public wards. That one dollar a day does not keep a patient in the hospital; the average of keep for the hospital may amount to $1.50 or $1.75 per day. Such a patient is not really a charity patient; he is paying the prescribed fee of the hospital; but at the same time he is living in an institution receiving aid from a Provincial Government, because the Provincial Government of Ontario-I do not know about Quebec-gives aid to these institutions such as general hospitals. I certainly do not agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) who said that the Government were attempting to dis-

franchise people because they were poor. I wish to disassociate myself from that criticism, because I do not think that is the intention of the Government.
The minister said so clearly.
If the clause I suggest were added to the clause, the whole point would be cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I would have no objection to adding a clause such as that suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) to the effect that "this section shall not apply to patients in hospitals, sanatoriums or other similar institutions who pay the fee from time to time prescribed by such institutions for patients."

Or give a certain
amount of money.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not go that
length. We have had experience under this section for a good many years, and we have had no trouble with it. I believe we shall have more difficulty if we change it than if we leave it as it stands.
New conditions have arisen since the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This section has never done any harm to anybody, and I think we are letting our imagination run away with Us. Some suggestions are good and some not so good. I am afraid, if we start meddling with this section, we shall get into more trouble than we have under it at present.
Why is the word "patient" to be used instead of the word "inmate" as used in the clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am not moving this as an amendment; I am just suggesting it.

In case the committee might misunderstand the meaning of the last suggestion, I may say that in many institutions there is no definite rate; the rate is governed by what the patient is able to pay. Very frequently, the medical doctor fixes the rate. Sometimes the parent will say that he can pay three dollars or five dollars or ten dollars a week for his child. There is no particular standard on which you can base a recommendation of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think we had better
let this clause remain as it is for a while.

There are many different kinds of charity. Supposing a charitable institution, such as the Red Cross Society, should take on a patient whom they want to

look after, and they could not find any place in which to put him except in sortie such institution as we have been discussing. They put him in that institution and they pay his board. He is not receiving public charity, but this association of charitable people undertakes to support him in that institution. If he is an intelligent man and is qualified to vote except that this association of charitable people is keeping him in that institution, I do not think that he should be deprived of his franchise. I should think that it would be better if the word "public" were inserted before the words "charitable support" wherever they appear in this clause. I know that in our province, since I remember anything about elections, a man who was getting money from the overseers of the poor, could not vote because he was receiving public aid, but that could not apply to a person who was a ward of a charitable institution such as I have described. There are two places in the section where the word "public" should be insei'ted before the word "charity," and I offer the suggestion to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to that amendment if it will make the section any clearer. The section is not intended to apply to private charities, but if the word "public" helps to make that intention more evident I do not mind inserting it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment of the hon. member for Three Rivers and St. Maurice (Mr. Bureau).

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that the insertion of the word "public" will serve the purpose better.
I do not know of any private institutions receiving aid from the Government in our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am inclined to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) and to insert the word "public" after the word "receiving" in the fourteenth and sixteenth lines.
The committee can dispose of only one amendment at a time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) will withdraw his amendment.
Mr. BURiElAU: I think the suggestion covers the point I have in mind. I beg to withdraw my amendment.
Amendment withdrawn.

speakerposition: subtopic
Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I now move to amend subclause (f) by adding the word "public" before the word "charitable" in lines fourteen and sixteen.

Will that meet the objection raised by the hon. member (Mr. Manion)? If a man pays so much a day in a hospital, to the upkeep of which the Government contributes some assistance, it might be argued that that man was receiving public charitable aid to some extent. 1 do not think that the proposed amendment meets the objection. Perhaps he will tell the committee whether he considers it satisfactory.

Will the hon. member (Mr. Manion) comply with that request? If a man did not pay the full fee charged private patients in a hospital that received support from the Government he might be considered to be receiving public charity in part. Does not my hon. friend think that the words "in part" in line fourteen should be omitted?

I must apologize to my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) for my apparent indifference to his question. I did not hear him. With regard to the' suggestion of the hon. member for Three Rivers and St. Maurice, I think it is a disputable point as to whether this provision would apply to patiepts in an ordinary general hospital, at least in any city in Ontario. I think the suggestion made by the minister is perfectly satisfactory.

W'e have agreed to put the word "public" after the word "receiving" and before the word "charitable" in the fourteenth and sixteenth lines. If my hon. friend will read the subclause he will see the purport of my suggestion.

It is not these lines to which I have reference; it is the last three lines of the section:
Or are inmates receiving charitable support in any institution receiving aid from the government of a province under any statute in that behalf.
The hospital receives a certain amount per day per patient. In Ontario, I think, it is fifty cents per day; so that if a patient in a public ward paid a dollar, that fifty cents would make up the difference between the cost of his ntaintenance and the amount he paid. It is questionable whether this clause would apply to such patients. In the elections in my constituency patients in the general hospital voted, and I cannot

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
COMMONS [DOT]
see that this clause would apply to such electors.
Mr. ROS'S: Does the .Acting Solicitor General think that the amendment he has moved meets the objection of the hon. member (Mr. Manion)?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It was not intended to.
Well, should it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that the section should stand as it is with the amendment proposed. The hospitals receive a per diem allowance per head from the Government. This is not for the maintenance of the individual patient; it is only a method by which is reached the amount which the hospital shall receive. When a patient pays his money to the hospital he is prima facie paying his way, and so far as I know his right to vote has never been challenged, and I doubt very much whether it ever will be. The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) raised a question as to persons receiving private charity. Private charity could not form a ground of disqualification, and it never was intended that it should. To meet the point raised by the hon. member, however, I move the adoption of the amendment which I have proposed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

In the second line of the same subclause there appear the words "criminal offences." I understand that the word "criminal" in this connection refers only to offences committed under certain statutes. What would be the status of a man who had been incarcerated for not having observed the temperance laws of Ontario? This man might be in jail where the hon. the Preseident of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) was running. If he should be condemned to jail under a federal statute he would be barred. But if he were condemned under a provincial statute would he be entitled to vote while the other man was prevented from voting? As the clause reads now an offender under a federal statute would be debarred, and I think that offenders under provincial laws and municipal by-laws should also be included.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it amounts to very much; if he is in jail, he is not going to vote.	,
I know a case where the prisoners "were allowed, under a sheriff's guard, to go and register their votes and they came back afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is a breach of the law. '

I wish to make myself perfectly clear to the committee in regard to the amendment I suggested, and whether I shall be supported or not, I am going to propose it. The clause is one which disqualifies certain electors. When wre come to subsection (g) we find that, notwithstanding the fact that certain provinces have disqualified a class of people on account of their race, we lift that disqualification from people of that particular race provided they have served in the naval, military or naval air forces of Canada. The purport of my amendment is that the same proviso be made on behalf of those who have served in the naval, military or air services of Great Britain or the Allies. If some hon. members prefer it I will simply put in "Great Britain" for the present, and necessarily and later on add the Allies. But in any case my amendment as it stands is to give the right to vote, notwithstanding racial disqualification, to anybody who wore the King's uniform and fought for the Empire during the late war.
I do not think I need to labour the point with members of this House. We heard during and after the war a great deal about the gratitude that was due to the soldiers from members of this House and others throughout the country. We recognized that in a substantial way when we gave certain rights to Imperial veterans in reference to pensions, and we recognized it in various other respects. It seems to me that we should give to people coming to this country the best welcome we can, and the best welcome we can give them is the right to vote, always provided that they are otherwise qualified. I could quote at length from the debates in this House in reference to this subject, but I will content myself -with calling attention to what the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) says, as reported at page 545 of Hansard, second session, 1919:
If he was a British subject and had at no time resided in this country, there was no place to which Parliament could with propriety allot his vote, and the only way to give him the franchise was to permit him to select his constituency.
Here we have a mail who was serving in the British army, who had never lived in Canada, and we told him that he could choose any constituency throughout the whole of Canada in which to vote. Further on the minister said:

Who is there who will stand up and say that British subjects who had sufficient interest in this country to come and join our armies and fight had not some right to say what should be the Government of this country during the war?
I could go on further and quote the remarks not only of the Minister of the Interior, but of a large number of members on both sides of the House, and particularly on the other side, but I think I have sufficiently explained my point, and I move in amendment:
That paragraph (g), clause 30, be amended by inserting, after the word " Canada '' in the 27th line, the words " Great Britain and the Allies."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I would like to ask my hon. friend what he has in mind. Has his proposed amendment any particular result ot is it academic? Does it refer to any people? If so, would he kindly let me understand something of his object?

My object is simply this, that by this Act we disfranchise, or we can disfranchise, certain British subjects who have seen service in the Imperial army. Whether there is one or a hundred, or five hundred in this country, I do not care.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Are there any?
The minister has told me that he knows of two.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Those are not disqualified; they are qualified under this section.
Two Hindus?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, who fought in the Canadian army.

I am quite sure that unless it he in British Columbia there are throughout the rest of the country a number of Hindu reservists who were called on and were ready to fight for the British flag at some place or other throughout the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is possible, but I have been informed that it is not so.

The law is to meet a general case. The province of Ontario might at some time or other, and possibly will, if we are to believe the reports of its rapid Americanization, take some means to disfranchise the negroes. Some other province might disqualify other races on account of Their colour, religion or language. I see no reason why people who have fought for the Empire should be disqualified on account of any particular prejudice that may exist in any province of the Dominion. I pre-116 J
sume that British Columbia is the only province which has the Hindu. I have no wish to interfere with the people of British Columbia, but I am convinced that the people of British Columbia themselves, knowing them as I do to have 'been very staunch supporters of the war and everything concerned in it, would not wish to exclude British subjects who were members of the British army or to prevent them from exercising the franchise. If the minister wishes me to go further I will add at the end of the paragraph the words "nor otherwise duly qualified dependents of such .members of the forces." Then the mother of the dead Hindu British subject, of the dead Chinese British subject, and of the dead Japanese British subject would be entitled to vote, and their widows, too. If the minister wishes, I will do that. If numbers are all he wants, we might get a few more in.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is just as well that the committee should know what my hon. friend's views on the subject are. If the object of his motion is to open up the question of the Oriental vote in this country and to leave the door as wide open as possible, as I judged from his concluding remarks, I disagree entirely.
No, I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If my information is
correct, and I think it is, within the present month of April the legislature of British Columbia, has expressly refused to allow' even returned soldiers of Oriental origin to vote. That is the information that has come to me. There is a popular impression both in the House and outside that in some way or other the mere fact that a man is a British subject entitles him to vote. That is wholly a wrong impression. British citizenship carries with it no right to vote. So far as I know, citizenship in no country carries with it the right to vote. The right to vote is a conferred right in every case. A man born within the shadow of Westminster may come to Canada and yet not be able to vote in the province of Nova Scotia. A British subject who has resided in Canada five years cannot vote in Nova Scotia unless he has certain qualifications which the legislature of that province says shall attach before he can vote. Citizenship of itself carries no right to the franchise. A certain number of Orientals did come to this country on our western coast, and they were naturalized. There is a popular impression, more particularly in the East,

that citizenship alone gives them the right to vote. I have heard it argued in this House that you are breaking your contract with a man who has a naturalization certificate if you do not give him the right to vote. This Parliament says upon what terms men shall vote. It is so in the United States and every other civilized country. We attach certain conditions. We say in the first place:	You must have
been-so many years in the country; secondly, you must have attained such and such an age, and in some parts of Canada, you must also have a property qualification. These requirements must all be cdmplied with before a man can vote. No Oriental, whether he be Hindu, Japanese or Chinese, acquires the right to vote in this country simply by the fact of citizenship. The Hindu is a British-born subject just as much as any Canadian, but he acquires no right by obtaining his certificate unless he can comply with all the other requirements of our law. I thought myself that when the province of British Columbia passed an Act to disqualify Orientals from voting they were going to the full extent of their constitutional power, if not over-stepping it. In fact I was very much surprised when the legislation was upheld by the highest court in the realm. The Imperial Privy Council held that the question of the franchise to be enjoyed within the province was a matter falling entirely within provincial rights and jurisdiction under section 93 of the British North America Act. Subsection (1) of section 93 provides that each province may regulate matters concerning its own constitution. The Privy Council held that the right to regulate the provincial franchise was a provincial constitutional right, and that the legislature had authority to vary or alter the requirements as it saw fit. Consequently, the Privy Council upheld the right of the province of British Columbia to say that an Orientp.1 should not vote, notwithstanding that he was a British subject. A year or two afterwards, we know, the legislature of that province passed another law prohibiting British subjects of Oriental extraction or origin from working in the mines under certain conditions, on underground work, I think it was. That Act was set aside by the Privy Council as ultra vires of the powers of the legislature of British Columbia. To my mind there is a great anomaly in those two decisions, but very able text-book writers have sought to reconcile them and have done so apparently to their own satisfaction, and evi-
dently the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council were satisfied. Personally, I believe it is a matter of very, very refined reasoning to distinguish the principles upon which these two opposing judgments are based. However, the law as it stands to-day and as interpreted is to the effect that a province can regulate its own franchise and can deprive a person otherwise qualified as a British subject of his right to exercise the franchise in provincial elections.
Whether the exclusion of the Oriental is right or wrong, I am inclined to think there is a very radical difference between the races of the Orient and the races of this hemisphere. I believe there is a great amount of truth in Rudyard Kipling's verse:
East is East and West is West, and never the twain shall meet.
The Oriental's ideas are different from ours; his training is different; his education is different; the habits and customs of the two people are different. I believe the greatest difference exists in regard to economic conditions, and that no doubt is the question which has caused all the trouble on our western coast. Their method of life is different from ours. They may be more industrious and more economical than we are. The labour question is at the bottom of the whole matter of the Oriental vote. The province of British Columbia has decreed in its wisdom that Orientals shall not vote on provincial affairs. We have merely carried out that provincial wish. I do not know that it is not somewhat anomalous for us to do so, but we have done it, and I believe that the proposal will come within the judgment of the House. We know, however, that certain portions of that Oriental community did serve with the Canadian forces in the war, and to that portion we are prepared to grant the franchise notwithstanding provincial disqualifications.

Is British Columbia
the only province in Canada that excludes Orientals from voting?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
British Columbia excludes Chinese, Japanese and Hindus. I aan informed that in Saskatchewan only Chinese are excluded. Now, I think the House will readily agree that men of Oriental extraction who served in the Canadian military, naval or air forces should have a vote. I cannot believe from any information I have, or from any information which my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. APRIL 29, 1920
Power) was able to give to the House, that there are any persons of Oriental extraction who served in the army of Great Britain or in the army of the Allies of Great Britain, and were otherwise qualified, who would be disqualified by this Act. An odd case might exist, but I have never heard of any. There is, however, just this difficulty.
