If you wish to extend this exception to the men who served in the armies of Great Britain and her Allies, Japan was an Ally, and a native of Japan who is living in British Columbia might have served in the army or navy of Japan, and under the amendment proposed by my hon. friend that man would have a right to vote. I do not think we are justified in going as far as that, because this amendment would not cover the case of men *who served in the army of the United 'States, which is not an allied but an associated power.

I will add "associated,"
right away.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
is rather exerting himself in an effort that is not going to get us anywhere. On academic and sentimental grounds I agree with him that the man who was good enough to fight our battles Is good enough to vote; we are together in principle and in sentiment so far as that goes. But I really think we are taking up too much time in matters that can have no practical result. There may be an odd man here or there who would be affected, but the result in any case is going to be very small. [DOT]

I do not intend to follow
my hon. friend the minister into a discussion of the racial and colour question in British Cblumbia or anywhere else. I have no knowledge of those conditions in British Columbia or Saskatchewan, and I am inclined to agree that whatever the people of those provinces think is best for themselves should be given effect to by this House. But we have already made an exception in favour of Canadian soldiers, and I think we should make similar exception in favour of a large number of soldiers of a racial origin different from ourselves who served in the Imperial army. It is all very well for the hon. minister to say that to his knowledge there are very few men who would be affected, but to my mind that does not alter the situation one bit. Either we were right in exempting our Canadian soldiers, or we were wrong; and the treatment meted out to a Canadian Hindu soldier, to a Canadian Japanese, or to a Canadian Chinese, should equally well he meted out to the British Chinese, soldier, the British
Hindu, and the British Japanese. Standing on that broad ground, I say that the minister should not object to the insertion of the words whichT wish to add.
I agree with the minister that the status of a British subject does not necessarily qualify him as an elector. But under section 29 we know who is qualified as an. elector: he must be a British subject of the full age of twenty-one years and resident in Canada. The man to wham I refer will have been a British subject, will have attained the full age of .twenty-one years, and will have been a resident of Canada; his only disqualification will be a racial one. You have already lifted this racial disqualification for the man who has served in the Canadian forces, and I ask you to lift it for him who has served in the British forces. We have allowed member of our force (to vote who had no interest whatsoever in Canada, except that they wore a Canadian uniform, and we have established a precedent by granting to those not otherwise qualified but British subjects the right to vote, provided they wore a uniform. Are we going to take away from those duly qualified now the right to vote, even though they do wear the uniform? I have heard the hon. minister quote Kipling with regard to the East and the West, but we also might quote the author of the Barrack Room Ballads with regard to another point:
For it's Tommy this, an' Tommy that, an' "Tommy, wait outside" ;
But it's "Special train for Atkins" when the trooper's on the tide,

On the surface there may appear to be a great deal in what the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Power) says. He has, however, given us the key to the situation when he states that he does not know the conditions in the Par West. If he were a citizen of the Pacific Province I am sure he would not have made his proposal. To use a mild word, Sir, that would be one of the most unfortunate amendments of the Franchise Act, and I dare not suggest what might be the outcome of such an amendment were the House to accept it. It is too absurd to be seriously considered.
Thank you.

I believe, with the minister, that the amendment is wrong in principle, and from our knowledge of the situation in the West, I am sure it would be a very unwise policy to adopt. The province of British Columbia has stated in very emphatic language its views on the matter of extending the franchise to Orientals. The

clause as framed goes as far, I believe, as it is safe or wise to go at the present juncture, and as the hon. gentleman, according to his own statement, does not really understand the position taken in the matter by British Columbia. I sincerely hope he will voluntarily withdraw his amendment and not ask the House even to express an opinion upon it by a vote.

I would like to hear from the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey) why it is absurd to give any British soldier a vote, and why it is more absurd to give a vote to a British soldier who served in the Imperial army than it is to give it to a British soldier who served in the Canadian army, if they both have the same racial characteristics. It can be more absurd to give the vote to the man who served with a Canadian shoulder-strap on his tunic than to the man who wore a turban. So far as the hon. gentleman is concerned, if the opinion of British Columbia coincides with his, and if that opinion has nothing more to back it up than what he has just stated, I am heartily glad that I know nothing of the conditions in that province.

It seems to me that subsection 2 of section 30 is very unhappily worded. It is difficult to understand what the draftsman meant. In the first half of that subsection it is made an offence for a . man to vote or to procure any one else to vote knowing that he or the other person is not qualified to vote, and that offence is punishable upon summary conviction as in the Bill provided. Then, the latter part of the subsection says:
On the trial of any person accused of having contravened this section by voting

Not by procuring any one else to vote.
-with knowledge of his disqualification, nonqualification or incompetency, the burden of proof as to all matters material shall be upon such person and not upon the Crown.
A man is charged with having voted when he was not qualified to vote. He is brought before a magistrate. If he says nothing, he is guilty, because the burden is upon him of proving everything against himself as well as in favour of himself. First, he would have to prove that he had
10 p.m. voted, and to do that he would have to produce the ballot papers and the poll book. I am satisfied that this subsection does not express what the draftsman had in mind and I think it had better stand for further consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I must thank my hon.
friend for having directed our attention to this clause. The Parliamentary Counsel has examined it and has pointed out that there is an error in it. After the word "in-eompeteney" in the 41st line there should be inserted the words "and upon proof that

the accused voted at such election/' and the word "other" should be inserted after the word "all' in the 42nd line.
* Should not the words "or procuring any other person to vote be inserted after the word "voting" in the 40th line? I think it is intended to include both.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That might improve it. As a matter of fact, it might be better to strike out after the word "section" in the 40th line the words "by voting with knowledge of his disqualification, non-qualification or incompetency"; to insert in lieu thereof the words "and upon proof that the accused voted at such election, and to insert the word "other" after the word "all' in the 42nd line.

In order to secure a conviction you still leave the burden upon the man accused to prove that he was not entitled to vote. The Crown establishes that he voted. If you stop there, there is no offence committed. Supposing the man says: "Well, I will just leave the matter where you left it." The man accused would still be required to prove bis own guilt by proving that he was disqualified from voting.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I see there are further difficulties in this clause, and it has evidently been improperly drafted. I think we shall let subclause 2 stand, because Mr. Gisborne's amendment does not meet the oase, and this might be a very important clause, particularly in regard to that provision w7hich permits men to be sworn in on election day for the purpose of voting.
Amendment withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Might I say just a word with reference to this feature of this legislation? If the enumeration principle is carried into 'this Bill and finally adopted, very careful provisions must be miade so that men cannot come forward and swear in their votes on election day. You must surround that privilege, if it exists, with every possible restriction and safeguard. As I understand it, the last subclause of this clause is to .provide that where a man whose name is- not on the list comes forward on election day and swears in his vote knowing that he has not a vote, then the burden of proof must be placed upon him at the trial to show that he had a vote.
The burden of proof is on any voter, whether he is on the list or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: I am not quite so sure about that. There are other offences mentioned in the first part of this clause, and as regards them the burden of -proof is on the Crown but in the case of the man. who knows that he had net a vote and who comes forward and swears in his vote, as regards that particular offence the intention is to place the burden of proof on him.
This is not confined to him at all; |t covers anybody.

I wish to congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) on his success in dealing with this clause. When this clause was under consideration on a former occasion, I took the very same objection as the hon. member has taken -and made a very strong argument. Of course, nothing good came out of that and I was wiped aside rwi'th a wave of the hand of the Minister of Militia.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This clause was never considered before.
I congratulate my hon. friend on having a better hearing than I had.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This clause was neveT considered before to-night.

I say that it was. Section stands.
On section 33-"when new lists of voters unnecessary:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There are some words left out here, and perhaps before considering the clause I had better have the clerical errors corrected. I move to amend clause 33 by striking out in the eighth line on page 24 the words "and to the revising officers;" by striking out in the tenth Mne on page 24 the word "print;" by striking out in 'the sixteenth line on page 24 the words "or revising officer;" and by inserting the word "rural" before the word "registrar" where the said word appears in the thirteenth and fifteenth lines on page 24.
That excludes registrars in cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

How -can the returning officer send a copy to each rural registrar if he has only three certified copies) Subclause 2 states that the Chief Electoral

Officer shall send three certified copies to the returning officer, and there may be twenty-five rural registrars.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move thalt clause 33 [DOT] be taken up, subclause by subclause and I think my hon. friend will see the bearing of this then.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
On section 33, subsection (1)-when new lists of voters unnecessary:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This subsection provides that it shall not be necessary, "except as otherwise provided in this section," to prepare new lists of voters for any election in any district when there has been in that electoral district a previous election for which the lists of voters prepared are of record in the office of the Chief Electoral Officer and there is an interval of less than twelve months between the dates of the writs for the two elections. I may point out that in subsection (3) the word "list" in line twelve should be in the plural.
Before the minister goes any futher, may I suggest that as this section is dependent on section 32 it should stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes.
Section stands.
On section 34-additional polling stations when more than 300 electors in a polling division:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There are some errors in this section which I desire to correct. In line 47 on page 24 of the Bill after the words "section thirty-two" the following words should be inserted "or by rule five of schedule B of said section"; and in line 32 after the word "registrar" there should be inserted the words "or revising officer." These, I think, are the only changes, and I move that the section be amended accordingly.

In line 31 it is provided: "The returning officer shall in such case direct the registrar to prepare .	. . from
the lists of voters ... a separate list." Should that not be the Chief Electoral Officer instead of the returning officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that is the duty of the returning officer.

If the Chief Electoral Officer in the first part of the section is authorized to direct the returning officer to prepare additional polling stations, why should he not also direct the returning officer to prepare this list?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In the first instance the returning officer determines the question.
On the advice of the Chief Electoral Officer, the Chief Electoral Officer authorizes or directs the returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Chief Electoral
Officer directs the returning officer, as regards the providing of additional polling stations only in cases where he sees fit; but where the polling division contains more than 300 voters the returning officer is bound to provide such stations. The clause directs that he "shall" do so.
Why is the [DOT] number 300 fixed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Because it is considered a reasonable number.

It takes a long time for electors to record their votes, and I should imagine that 250 would be a reasonable number to fix as the maximum for a polling division. My hon. friend knows that a large number of women will exercise the franchise for the first time in the next election, and as they will not be as adept at voting as men, it will take a good deal of time for them to cast their votes.
Mr. BElLAND : And certain courtesies will have to be shown them.

Exactly, and as they cannot be stampeded it is only natural to expect that a good deal of time will be required. If we intend to crowd in forty or fifty voters in an hour some very fast work will have to be done by the deputy returning officer and the officials at the polls. It is only for the sake of convenience that I make this suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that 300 is a reasonable number. We desire to keep down the number of officials as far as possible, and the Act as it is will be fairly expensive. I do not think there is any difficulty in polling 200 votes in a division. There may be odd hours in the day when there is a rush, but it is slow work to poll only 200 votes. The polls are open from six in the forenoon until six at night, a matter of twelve hours.

I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Power). From experience I know that it is a matter of difficulty for a great many voters to go to thS polls early in the day, and there is generally a considerable rush towards the close of the day. I therefore think that 250 would be a sufficient number of electors for any polling division, es-

pecially in view of the extra time which it will take to accommodate the ladies.

This gives roughly one vote polled every two and a half minutes. It is true this was under the old Act; but under the old Act in certain portions of the country the lists were old and we could reasonably suppose that a large number of those whose names were on the list were dead or absent or otherwise could not vote. But the lists here are essentially up-to-date.
Hear, hear.

If we were going into a discussion of that I think that perhaps we would be able to convince the minister that the lists are too much up-to-date. In any case we can reasonably suppose that the whole 300 who are on the list will wish to vote, and as I have said this means a vote polled every two and a half minutes.
I submit that two and a half minutes per person is not sufficient. It would be very easy for an evil-disposed deputy returning officer, aided by an evil-disposed election agent, to block a poll for the last two or two and a half hours. I do not know whether the minister has ever heard of the procedure of blocking the poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Never.
As I understand it happens in the best regulated families.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You cannot block them in Ontario.

If the minister would go to some other provinces in Canada he could, if he wished, learn a great deal in regard to the very ingenious procedure which they have in order to manipulate elections. There is no doubt it can be done. It should be very easy to say and amend this clause to fix the number at 250 voters.

It is provided in line 35 that these lists shall be made in alphabetical order, and it is provided further that when there are two polls in one polling subdivision one list shall proceed from (a) to (k) or from (1) to (r) and so on. That is quite proper, but I would like to have this point elicited at once: How will a married woman's name be entered on the voters' lists?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Section 32 provides for that.
It does not provide how her name shall be entered.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, with a "W" after it.
The "W" will indicate that she is a married woman?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No. Paragraph (a) of Rule 6, page 18 says:
Such list shall show the names thereon alphabetically arranged according to surnames-
And so on.

Mary Smith is married to Edward Hall,-how will Mary Smith's name be entered on the list? Will it be Mrs. Edward Hall; will it be Mrs. Mary Smith Hall, which is a form adopted sometimes; will it be Mrs. Mary Hall; will it be Mrs. Mary Smith, or will it be Mrs. Mary Smith wife of Edward Hall? It could be designated on the list in five different ways which would change the alphabetical order.
I would ask the minister whether the way in which a married woman will be designated on the list is provided for anywhere in the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. There is provision made for it, although the provision might have to be made clearer in section 32. The list is to be prepared under subsection (a) of rule 6, page 18. The list itself is to be prepared and completed in accordance with form ,(k'), page 82. The form contains spaces for "name," "occupation or addition" and "residence". The form prescribed in the case of a single woman is: "Miss Mary Baker" and in that of a married woman "Mrs. Ann Dow". "W" follows t'he name of each and also "spinster" or "married woman" or "widow". That is the form to be followed under section 32. But I think we are wasting time in considering section 32 as I am under a promise not to discuss it to-night.
On page 82, form 4, we see "Mrs. Ann Dow". Is this lady's maiden name Dow, or is Dow the name of her husband?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Why?
Because the law says that a married woman shall take the surname of her husband.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) is right, but the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) is of some importance. I know that in my election in Quebec East last fall the registrar had entered the maiden name of women with the annotation "wife of" such and

such a man. The husband and wife, when coming to poll their votes, had to register their votes at separate polls on account of that arrangement. That was wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: When we again come to section 32 we can make that clear. .
That is the legal way of designating married women in our province according to the code of civil procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is not the legal way under the statutes of this Parliament.
In our province we designate a married woman by her maiden name and put "wife of so and so".

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the Federal law a woman takes the name of her husband.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 35-who shall not be appointed election officers:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is one word to be added, although it is not very important. I move to amend clause 35 by inserting the word "registrar" after the words "returning officer" in the second line of the said clause.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 36-writ of election, indexed copies of this Act, blank poll books and forms, to be sent to returning officer :

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Chief Electojal Officer, or Parliamentary Counsel, has suggested an amendment there in reference to the franking privilege. It should be granted to the Chief Electoral Officer as he will have a good deal of matter to send out by mail just at the time of the election. I beg to move:
All letters or mailable matter addressed to the Chief Electoral Officer, at Ottawa, or sent by the said Chief Electoral Officer, from Ottawa, shall be free of Canadian postage under such regulations as the Postmaster General shall prescribe.
This amendment was prepared by the Post Office authorities.
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
_ Oo section 37-proclamation by returning officer mailed to postmasters:

When this section was under consideration before, I asked that the proclamations be printed in both French and English not only in the province of Quebec and Manitoba, but in all the pro-

vinces. This is a bilingual country and we may as well recognize that fact at once. We should not allow the small additional expenditure that would be involved to stand in the way. In this year of billions we need not consider a few hundred dollars if the expenditure is to satisfy the whole people of Canada. It would not be necessary or advisable, I think, to have the proclamations in both languages in British Columbia at the present time, but I think it should be done in all the other provinces. Ontario has a French population of nearly 300,000, one-third of the population of New Brunswick is French, and in some districts of that province there are only one or two English families. In the whole Maritime Provinces there will be a population by the next census of 180,000 French-speaking people. I trust the minister will have the proclamations printed in both languages for all the provinces except British Columbia. I mentioned this when the clause was under consideration before, and I hope the minister is prepared to-night to accept my suggestion. The clause could be so worded as to leave it to the discretion of the returning officer in English-speaking centres where there were only a few French residents, to decide whether the proclamations were required in both languages.

I wish to endorse the
suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon). During the last election I was approached by several of the officers in my constituency to help them translate their instructions from English into French, so that they could understand their duties on polling day. A few days before polling day I had to send certain parties from one poll to another in order to help the officers holding the polls to understand their instructions, which were printed in the English language. In my constituency there are several polls where you will find not more than one or two English families. Everything official is done more or less in the French language and has to be translated into English, and this it is very difficult for some of them to do. The returning officer appointed for my constituency at the last election could not read French, and consequently he had great difficulty in giving the proper instructions to the different officers at the polls throughout the constituency. I trust that the minister will accept the suggestion of my hon. friend to have the proclamations printed in both languages.

I have very much pleasure indeed in supporting the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon). I spoke on this

question when the clause was under consideration a few nights ago. There are a great many districts in the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island where the population is mostly all French. In the county I have the honour to represent, three-quarters of the population are French-speaking, and in a great many parishes of the county there are no English-speaking people at all. I therefore think it only right that the proclamation should be printed in both languages so that the electors will know what they mean. Women now have the right to vote, and they should know what is going on. Not many of them in our part of the country can read English, but they can read French, and it would be very convenient to them and the public generally to have these proclamations printed in French as well as English. The expense would not be very great. We could leave it to the discretion of the returning officers to decide whether proclamations in both languages were required at certain polls.

I presume this clause applies to Quebec and Manitoba because the French language is by the constitution of the British North America Act and by the Manitoba Act official in the courts of these provinces. Since these Acts were passed there has been a large increase in the French population in other provinces, particularly in Ontario and some of the Maritime Provinces. In some constituencies of Ontario a large majority of the population is French-speaking, so I think tlm Bill should be amended to provide for the issue of the proclamation in both languages in constituencies where there is a considerable French-speaking population. Power could be given to the Chief Electoral Officer to instruct the returning officer to issue the proclamations in both languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This is one of the
clauses that have received very earnest consideration from the Government. Personally I sympathize very much with hon. members who have spoken of the difficulties which arise in various parts of the province of New Brunswick, and perhaps other parts of the Dominion, from the fact that our people are not so well educated as to be masters of both French and English. It would be far better for us all if we were; unfortunately we are not. I think we all realize that the language question has heretofore excited a marked difference of opinion, and undoubtedly the Government has acted wisely in deciding to abide by the established rule. The two provinces of
Quebec and Manitoba are specially mentioned in this section and in another section, but the reason is that there are constitutional questions in both these provinces in regard to the right to use the French language which do not exist in the other provinces. There may be some slight inconvenience in some parts of the country by reason of the fact that the clause is not more extensive in its operation, but I think there are rights on both sides in respect to this question, and it is far wiser and safer for the Government to follow well-known and approved paths than to enter upon any new ventures of a very controversial nature on the matter of convenience in elections.

Although this clause may
have been in force for a long time, I think some changes are now due. Our population has increased considerably not only in New Brunswick but in several other of our provinces, and therefore I think we must change our law to accommodate our people.
I for one am sorry that all our people cannot read and speak the English language, and although no doubt with the spread of education our young people do not labour under that disadvantage, their parents have not had the same opportunities, and they should be considered in a matter of this kind. I appeal to the Government to make the change now; it would not hurt anybody, the expenditure would not amount to anything, and it would satisfy a great many people throughout the country.

There is an old saying
that if you give a man an inch he wants a mile.

I do not want a mile, I
only want what is just and right.
You conclude from that to give him nothing?

No. I mean there is
nothing in the British North America Act that would warrant inserting in this Bill authority to use the French language in Manitoba.

There is that authority
in the Manitoba Act.
No.

It is all through the
Dominion, and this is Dominion legislation.

No. Section 133 of the
British North America Act defines the matter pretty well.
The regulations in connection with this Bill are supposed to be written in both French and English.
No.
Why not? The official languages are French and English.

No. The French language cannot be imposed upon any province except there is' legal right to impose it. Section 23 of the Manitoba Act of 1870 defines the rights to the use of the French language in Manitoba:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the Houses of the Legislature, and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person, or in any pleading or process, in or issuing from any court of Canada established under the British North America Act, 1867, or in or from all or any of the courts of the provinces. The Acts of the Legislature shall be printed and published in both those languages.
That I conceive, Mr. Chairman, to constitute the limits of that right. No possible right can arise that exceeds the express words of the statute. I do not think that the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger) contends that there is any right, constitutional or otherwise, to use the French language in his province. As I understand the history of this section, it was put in our election law many years ago by -Sir John Macdonald's government, and was allowed to remain there by the government of Sir-Wilfrid Laurier, the limitations apparently being acceded to, as were the concessions. This section does not abrogate any of the rights that were heretofore confirmed or granted, but the moment this Bill comes before the House hon. gentlemen seek to obtain similar privileges or concessions in respect to other portions of the Dominion.
Is there anything wrong in doing so?

I do not say there is
very much wrong in doing so, but there is no reason why a wrong should be granted either as of right or of grace.
Can a wrong be granted as a right?

My hon. friend, being
Irish, will probably get that through his brain sometime after he quiets down from the disturbing effects of this debate.
That will be just as soon as the hon. gentleman himself gets it through his brain.

The point is, the right established by that section. This Parliament has no constitutional right to go any further in legislation of this kind. As hon. 
members are aware, the British North America Act defines the rights of this Parliament. I have not section 133 of that Act at hand, but it limits the use of the French language as an official language to the province and the Legislature of Quebec, to the Dominion House of Commons, and to all Federal courts established by the Dominion Government, namely, the Supreme Court and the Exchequer Court.
I do not raise this question for the purpose of sowing seeds of discord or for depriving' any section of our people of what might seem to them to be a special privilege; but merely to point out to the hon. member for Kent, N.B., that he presumes that such a right exists in his province. I do not think we should let those presumptions go unchallenged when we know the law is dead against them; and as the law has been in this form for so many years I see no reason why it should be changed now.

I do not think -it is fair to say that if the Government gives us an inch we want a mile. All the people of the country, whether they are French, English, Irish or any other nationality, are entitled to their rights. Rules and regulations should be -adjusted to meet the -growth of the country, and I do not see that there should be any exception in this case. The people of the French race speak French and it -is of no use to try to prevent them from doing so; life is too short to make that worth while. Likewise the people of the English race speak English, and it is useless for the French people to try to prevent them from speaking English. We have to take the situation as it stands, and I believe that the Government will be generous enough to allow the minority in any province the rights to which -they are entitled. I am not asking for favours; I am asking only for what is a matter of right to Frenchspeaking people.
My hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) has read section 133 of the British North America Act-.

I did not read it; I
quoted it from memory.

Well, I will read it. My hon. friend's memory is very good because he used the exact words of the section, and I want to use those very words against him. Section 133 reads:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the Houses of the Parliament of Canada and of the Houses of the Legislature of Quebec; and

both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those Houses.
The records and proceedings in connection with an election are returned to the Chief Electoral Officer and form part of the records of this Parliament. Clause 75 of the Rill provides that the Chief Electoral Officer shall keep these papers in his possession for at least one year, and, if the election is contested, for one year after the termination of such contestation. The Chief Electoral Officer cannot move an inch without the authority of this Parliament. If, therefore, these papers are records of this House, it is the duty of the returning officer to use both languages. Further, it is provided by section 37 that certain papers shall be issued "in the English language only in other electoral districts" than those in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba. Why should there be such a provision if the right to have these records printed in the French language is not recognized? I repeat that these papers form part of the records of this House, and that the records of this House must be kept in both languages; therefore my hon. friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Leger) asks for a right, not a favour. Hon. gentlemen say that when we get an inch we want a mile, but the fact is that they are depriving us of something we are entitled to.

How does this clause
compare with the section of the Act under which the election of 1911 was conducted?

I have not compared them, but the Acting Solicitor General says that they are the same, and I am willing to take his word for it. But I understand that this Act is supposed to be an improvement on the old Act.

Then in what respect
does.this section deprive any portion of the people of any right that they formerly possessed?

That is not the point. If we have been deprived of any right it should be restored to us. Two blacks do not make a white, nor two evils a right. The member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) seems to think that he is extending great favours to us, whereas he is really depriving us of rights to which we are entitled. Relying on the British North America Act, he argues that we are not entitled to certain rights; I say that we are
11 p.m. entitled to them under that veTy Act. The fact that the restriction was in the old Act makes no difference.
I care not whether it was put there by Liberals or Conservatives. I say, where the law is good, do not change it, but where it can be improved, we are entitled to offer criticisms and suggestions. We hate to be told when we make a suggestion that it is hollow, or that when we speak it is only mockery. We do not want to be treated flippantly and told that favours are being extended to us when we complain that we are being deprived of some of our rights.

I have not been able to observe in the discussion of this clause a disposition on the part of any hon. member which would warrant the remarks which my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) has just made.
I am told that this section is worded precisely the same as the sections which have governed this matter for years. Now, let us go no further back than 1911. Who was re- . sponsible for the framing of the Act at that time? The late Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. If under that Act any of the people were deprived of their rights, the member for Three Rivers and St. Maurice (Mr. Bureau) and other hon. gentlemen had an opportunity to place their views before the then Prime Minister and to have the Act so .amended as to grant them the rights which they now claim under the constitution.
I think I may take it pretty well for granted that if the argument of these hon. gentlemen was good, that they were entitled under the constitution to any other rights than they have under this clause and than they have had under the section of which this is an exact copy, they would have put up their claims before this and their claims would have been recognized. Therefore, I take it that is pretty conclusive proof that they had no such constitutional right. There are a number of Freneh-Cana-dians in Ontario and in a number of the other provinces. Hon. gentlemen claim that the two languages should be recognized in every province of the Dominion; but in the western provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, there are people of other races, speaking other languages, who are more numerous than are the French-Canadians in those provinces. Should we recognize their claim that they cannot read the proclamation which is put up in English and say that, therefore, it should be put up in German, Polish, Austrian, and several other languages? Oh, no; hon. gentlemen will say that their language stands on a different plane. So it does in certain parts and in certain records

of the country; but from the constitutional standpoint, it does not stand on any different plane whatever except in those provinces which have been specifically mentioned, and hon. gentlemen are asking for something to which they are not entitled. In New Brunswick, where there are a number of French-Canadians, when an election came on, the proclamation was put up in the English language and they managed to get along with that ten, fifteen, twenty years ago. If they could do that, they should be able to get along better to-day - than twenty years ago, because if the schools of New Brunswick have been conducted along proper lines, every one of the electors of the younger generation in that province should be able to speak or read the English language. These hon. gentlemen will not claim that they have any right? to bilingual schools in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. If they have not been endeavouring in those provinces to keep their children away from the English schools and if they have not been running schools of their own, their children, now grown up to manhood and voting age, should be able to read any proclamation issued in the English language. I see no reason from a constitutional standpoint why this clause should be changed and made to read differently from the way in which it has read in past years. If there were any constitutional right, I believe the section would have been changed long ago, and the fact that it was not changed seems to indicate that the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier felt that there was no constitutional right on which to base a change of that section and'consequently he left it as it was and as it is now.
Surely my hon. friend has no objection to the proclamations and pther documents relating to an election being printed in French so that they might be better understood?
Would my hon. friend raise any objection to changing this clause so as to make it compulsory for the proclamation To be printed in forty or fifty languages throughout the western part of the country?

That is not the question at all.
Mr. EDW1ARDS: I am asking my hon. triend a question. I answered my hon. friend's question before by stating that there was no constitutional right, as I understand it, for printing the proclamation [Mr. Edwards. 3
in the two languages other than where is mentioned in this clause, and I doubt very much whether there is a constitutional right to printing it in two languages in 'Manitoba.
Mr. LEMiIEUX: May I recall to my hon. friend that some years ago the Indians of Canada were enfranchised, and at that time the proclamation was published in the Indian language in the county of Haldimand?
Mr. LElGER: il am surprised to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards), in order to justify his contention that the proclamation should not be printed in the French language, argue that in 1911, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power, this change was not made. Many things were not done at that time which should be done now, and perhaps at that time no one asked for this change. It is nine years since 1911 and many changes have taken place in Canada. We have had a war since then which has made many changes. In 1911 the cost of living was low whereas to-day it is almost as high as it can possibly go. I do not see much force in my hon. friend's arguments when he says: Why was this not done when the Liberal party was in power? Every year the laws of the country, are amended to a certain extent. Why, then, cannot this law be amended the same as any other law? I believe the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) is willing to make this change notwithstanding the argument put forward oy my hon. friend.

Does my hon. friend
think that the minister would have the right, under the constitution, to order the proclamations printed, let us say, in Manitoba or Saskatchewan, in English and Hungarian, in English and Austrian, in English and Polish, in English and Italian, or in English and several other languages?

That is no argument. The hon. member knows perfectly well there are two official languages in the Dominion of Canada. Why then does he bring in the question of other languages in order to try to dodge the point? I do not think that is any fair argument for an hon. member to make. We have the two official languages in this House and throughout the country. That being the case, to ask whether we would be willing that the proclamation should be printed in fifty languages is childish argument.

I was surprised at the remarks of my hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) who possesses a commendable knowledge of the French language and who greets me every morning and holds a friendly conversation with me in that tongue. I did not expect that he would give me the cold shoulder in connection with this proposal I have made; I expected quite the opposite from him. I see no reason for any comparison between the French language and German or Austrian or any other foreign language. There are only two official languages in this country, English and French, and what else are we doing in this Parliament if not recognizing the fact that Canada is a bilingual country? I am not an extremist by any means, and I never use any extreme arguments; but I can say without the least fear of being accused of exaggeration that the province of New Brunswick, so far as harmony between its French-speaking and Englishspeaking people is concerned, is a model to the whole of Canada. The French constitute one-third of the population of that province, and if the amendment which I move were accepted by this House it would afford additional grounds for the admiration which the people of my race in the province from which I come have for the British Crown and British institutions. Let me say that we are inspired in our devotion to the Mother Country not so much by the cries of Ontario as by the knowledge that we can rely on British justice for our rights in the future

those rights may be delayed, but they will not be denied. Things have been improving in Canada since Confederation, and to-day we are preparing a new law which will have a far-reaching effect on our political life. Why not therefore endeavour to make it as perfect as possible? This is a time when people are aiming at efficiency and perfection since the destruction which the war has wrought, and I think the present is a most appropriate occasion for the adoption of such an improvement in legislation of this kind as I am now proposing. By the Constitution of Canada we have two official languages in this country. Is there any reason, therefore, why this amendment should not be accepted? The question of expense which might be involved ought not to weigh in the consideration of this matter. Expenditures are after all of no account when the happiness, both present and future, of the people of this country is at stake. We must consider the future harmony which should exist in this country, and if this amendment were adopted it would make for a vast improvement in the relations that exist between the French and English elements in our population. I am not asking for any privilege for foreign people. Any immigrant not of English or French origin coming to Canada is supposed to have a general knowledge of the laws of this country, and he comes here well aware that there are only two languages,which are officially recognized. He must therefore make up his mind to adapt himself to this condition, and I am sure that if the people of the country were encouraged to learn both French and English there would be a great improvement in their social relations. If there were the same amicable intercourse between the French and English people of the upper provinces as there is between the two races in the province of New Brunswick there would be no lurking suspicions in the minds of either class. In my province Protestant and Catholic walk together on their way to their respective churches and part at the corner with the best feelings toward one another, and this is the spirit which I should like to see exist throughout this fair Dominion. If the Government could realize what a great step this amendment would be towards better harmony and good-will in the country, I cannot help thinking that they would-be inclined to accept it. In the province of British Columbia the French-speaking population is practically nil, and I would not ask that proclamations should be issued in both languages there. In New Brunswick we also have constituencies where there are no French people, and in those places it would not be necessary to have the proclamations printed in French. But in every district where there are any num-

ber of French people I certainly think that the proclamations should be printed in both languages. My hon. friends opposite know sufficient of human nature to realize that this amendment if adopted would be regarded as evidence of a spirit of conciliation on their part. Now that we are making a new franchise law let us see to it that it contains every provision that will be acceptable to the people as a whole. I now move that section 37 subsection (1) be amended to read as follows:
Within two days after the receipt of the writ of election the returning officer shall, by a proclamation in form L issued under his hand in the English and French languages and mailed one copy at least to the various postmasters of the post offices within his electoral district.

I rise to add a few words to the argument made by my hon. friend from Three Rivers and St. Maurice (Mr. Bureau). The hon. member cited section 133 of the British Nortih America Act, which provides that both languages shall be used in respect of the records and of the Journals of the Houses. I believe he has stated rightly that the proclamation of the returning officer constitutes a part of the records and that these records should be made in both languages. But, I shall go further. Section 133 says:
The Acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
It seems to me that the forms that generally accompany an Act and are contained in the schedule form part of the Act. Section 37 of the Bill says:
Within two days after the receipt of the writ of election the returning officers shall, by a proclamation in form L-
And so on. If I read form L, page 86, in connection with this Act, I find the proclamation itself in French in the French version and as section 133 of the British North America Act says'that the Act shall be printed and published in both languages, it seems to me that it applies to the forms. They shall be printed in both languages, the Act says, but they shall also be published. It does not mean that they shall only be published in this House or in Parliament, but it means that publication will be made wherever the Act is applied. I believe this is another argument in favour of the constitutional right. But even if we were not standing on firm ground regarding the constitutional right, although I believe we are, the right hon. the Acting Prime Miniser (Sir George Foster) has been preaching harmony and the bonne entente between the two races,

and I think if he had been here to-night he would have got up and chastised the ho-n. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) for denying us our rights, thus preventing the bonne entente between the different races in Canada. I do not believe I have anything else to add although I would like to allay the fears of my hon. friend from North Perth by- telling him that we do not ask that this proclamation should be printed and published in Parisian French but simply in good Canadian French.

Mr. Chairman, while listening to what has been said on this question, I would preface what I have to say by remarking that I do not agree with the constitutional claim that is made by the speakers on the Opposition aide as to their rights in this case. Neither do I .agree with the extent to which the amendment goes; that is that French .should be used in all the provinces. But, realizing as I do that we are trying here to make .a fair Act, I do think that we might agree to a proposition of this kind because we will always have, before the election, the census returns showing those constituencies wherein there is a large French vote. Recognizing, what .we all recognize, that the French tongue has a place in this land beyond all other languages outside of the English language I think we might, where there is a large proportion of French speaking people, grant the right of requiring that the proclamation should be published in the French as well as the English tongue. That would apply to a part of the province of New Brunswick; probably, to parts of the province of Saskatchewan; certainly to parts of .the province of Manitoba, and certainly to parts of the province of Ontario. Let me add, in regard to this- because as politicians or members of Parliament, we always have to guard ourselves about our statements-I 'think I have only 240 French-speaking people altogether in my constituency, which means so small a vote that I would not strengthen myself in the constituency by appealing to it to 'the disregard of others. But I am speaking of what is fair under this law.

I had felt that I would not be waiting in v.aiin to hear some authorized voice from the other side of 'the House in response to the request-the almost pathetic request-made to the committee by the 'three hon. members from New Brunswick. When this clause first came under consideration the hon. member foT Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) and his two hon. colleagues from

New Brunswick represented to the committee that in their respective constituencies, as in a number of other constituencies in the province of New Brunswick, there were a large number of (Canadian citizens not conversant with the English language. They have therefore, in a very moderate tone indeed, requested the minister to consider thedr proposition. Up to the present moment, although the request has been repeated oftentimes on this side of the House no horn, gentleman on the other side has judged it proper to express his acquiescence.
I was extremely sorry to hear the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy)-a personal friend of mine, I hope,-and also my hon. friend the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). They have sought refuge, as an excuse for their opinion, (behind the constitution. I would not like to press the claim put forth by my hon. friends from New (Brunswick on the exclusive ground of the British North America Act but if you bear in mind that the proclamation for the federal election is an its nature and of necessity a federal document you must at the same time admit that it should be published in both languages. The constitutional point has been made quite strongly by my hon. friend from Three Rivers and St. Maurice (Mr. Bureau) and has been accentuated, and properly accentuated, by my hon. friend from Chambly and Ver-cheres (Mr. Arehambault). Is it denied that it is a federal document? The hon. member for North Perth, I think, asked the question whether it would be proper, for instance, to print the proclamation in French in an English or an almost entirely English province.
Mr. (MORPHY: No, I did not ask that.
Mr. BEtLAND:	Well, something to that
effect. The hon. member for Frontenac thought that in a province where the large majority was English it would not be proper to print the proclamation in French. It is not a provincial document, I must repeat; it is a federal document which is printed, and published by the authority of a federal officer, whose existence we provide for in the present Act. Let us suppose for one moment that there is no strictly constitutional right for the printing of the proclamation in both languages. Here is a country where there are mainly two great races, the English and the French, the French being in a large majority in one of the provinces and being a very small minority in Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, (Saskatchewan and Alberta. A Franchise Bill is brought down for the 117
consideration of this House, and therein it is provided that the proclamation shall be printed in French in. two of the provinces only. The ground taken is that the old Act so provided. What of it? Have not the conditions changed? Who can say that there are no more Canadians of the French tongue in New Brunswick to-day than there were fifteen years ago? And the same thing applies to Ontario and Saskatchewan, and perhaps some of the other provinces. The only reason that is given for imposing this clause to-day is that the old Act provided that the proclamation should be printed in both languages in two provinces only.
What do we say? We say that while no complaint was laid before Parliament before, to-day, one is presented in a most appealing manner by my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon) and his two colleagues from New Brunswick. What do they ask? They state first to the House: We have in our province a number of Canadian citizens who are not conversant with the English language; they cannot read the proclamation in English; and we therefore ask, we beg of you, that in these districts, populated largely by French Canadians, the proclamation shall be printed in both languages. The only ground on which that request could be refused, not being unconstitutional, would be the ground of economy. What economy could be effected by printing a proclamation in only one language? Only a trifle, at most. I expected, and I say so candidly and frankly, that the suggestion would be accepted immediately. What does my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon) ask for? What has he claimed? True, his amendment as you read it would mean the printing of the proclamation in both languages in all of the provinces, but if I heard his remarks aright, he said:	Leave it to the
discretion of the -Chief Electoral Officer to decide outside of Quebec and Manitoba in what electoral districts the proclamation shall be printed in both languages. He does not ask the exclusively English-speaking districts of Ontario or the West or the Maritime Provinces to read the proclamation in French. No, he does not go as far as that. What he asks is most reasonable. Present to the electors, he says, who are not conversant with the English languages in other provinces of the Dominion a proclamation that they can read if they are French-speaking citizens. The question was asked by my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards). Would you print the proclamation



in ten, twenty, thirty or forty different languages for the western provinces? That question has already been answered.
I should like to hear my hon. friend answer it.
My hon. friend will not deny that the French language stands in a position by itself in Canada, outside, of course, the English language.

[DOT] Silence on my part would mean acquiescence, and I do not want my hon. friend to think that I acquiesce in his statement as he puts it, because I certainly do not. I recognize, just as well as my hon. friend or any other hon. member of this House, that by the Constitution the French language is given a different position from every other language in this country except English. The position occupied by the French language is clearly set down in the constitution. That is what I claim, and I claim that the French language has been recognized according to the Contitution of the country so far as the Constitution warrants. From the constitutional standpoint I want to tell my hon. friend that I do not appreciate that the French language has any different status from any other language out in the West or in any other part, so far as this amendment is concerned. You may ask for it on sentimental grounds, if you like.

From the constitutional
standpoint I want to take clear issue with my hon. friend. The French language is officially recognized in the British North America Act. Outside of the English language is there any other language except French mentioned in the British North America Act?
That is all right, I recognize that.
That does not agree with what my hon. friend contends. He contends that the French language has no different standing in Canada from the Austrian language.
I did not contend anything of the kind.
By implication.

I do not think my hon. friend would intentionally misrepresent me, but he is misrepresenting me. I have read the British North America Act and I know the rights to the use of the French language in this House. I know that it has equal rights with the English 
language in this House and in the courts, and so on, and that no other language has that right. My hon. friend is not representing me fairly when he makes me say that I do not recognize the French language as occupying any different position from any other language in this country. I have recognized that.
I am most happy that my hon. friend has now admitted that the French language enjoys in Canada a different position from other foreign languages.
I have never said otherwise.

I understood my hon.
friend to claim that the French language had no different standing in Canada from other foreign languages. He asked a question of some hon. gentlemen on this side, " Would you stand, then, for the printing of the proclamation in forty or fifty different languages in the West?" In answer to that question, I do not stand for the printing of the proclamations in forty or fifty different languages, but I claim that, if not absolutely in accordance with the strict provisions of the constitution, it would be only British fair play in view of history, and in view of the constitution as it stands as regards Quebec and Manitoba, to say to the French-speaking sections of this country: When you are called upon to register your vote in a general election you will be able to read the proclamation in your own language if you are a Frenchman, because you were the pioneers in this country, and with us framed Confederation.
In view of what happened at the opening of this session, in view of the magnificent speech delivered in French by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), and the subsequent speech he made, which was one of the finest appeals I ever heard from the mouth of any hon. gentleman of this House, in favour of harmony and bonne entente, I would expect that this request would be immediately granted. In New Brunswick, in Nova Scotia, in Ontario, and in some of the western provinces there are old folk who had no opportunity to learn English. Why should you deprive them of the privilege of reading in French the proclamation of a general election? And you cannot be condemned for granting them that privilege-certainly not on constitutional grounds. You may say: ''The constitution does not force me to grant it." But no hon. gentleman, .1 submit, can state that you are precluded by the constitution from doing so; such a con-

tention would not hold. You can grant this privilege. It has been asked for by the representatives of large French-speaking sections, and I hope my hon. friend will see his way clear to accept, not necessarily the amendment suggested by my hon. friend, but an amendment providing that m sections where the French language is largely used, in whatever province it may be, the proclamation shall be printed both in English and in French. This is a reasonable request. I do not believe that I have ever pressed in this House a request that was not absolutely reasonable. My hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon)- whom all hon. members know and have learned to appreciate-has never pressed in this House any request that wajs not fair and reasonable. What can you lose in granting it? Nothing. What can you gain? The development in the French sections of this country of a spirit of friendship and bonne entente the like of which you have never experienced before.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened to the discussion with the greatest of interest, and speaking for myself, I must say that in the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) there is sufficient I think to warrant me in saying that it is deserving of the fullest consideration on the part of the Government, and in that view I would ask that this section be allowed to stand. I must make myself clear, however, I would not approve the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon), but I think it worth while that we should have further consideration of a question which divides public opinion as this certainly does. The suggestion that perhaps the Chief Electoral Officer might determine whether the proclamation should be issued in French, or in English, or in both languages, is one that should be fully considered before the matter is finally decided. I express no opinion on the matter in the meantime; I merely ask that it be allowed to stand until I have had a chance to discuss it with my colleagues.

I do not press my
amendment as worded; my ambition is that the right of having proclamations issued in both languages should be accepted as a matter of expediency and nothing else. As my hon. friend (Mr. Beland) has stated, I do not ask that the proclamation should be issued in French in every constituency, even in New Brunswick; in British Columbia we do not expect it. The amendment could be so worded that it would not oper-1171
ate in constituencies where the population is entirely English-speaking. It is only in French constituencies or in mixed constituencies that I would like to have this amendment put in force. With this explanation I hope that my hon. friend who has charge of this Bill will be able to bring down an amendment which will be acceptable to us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Gloucester desire to withdraw his amendment?
No, it stands.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Acting Solicitor General moves that clause 37 and the proposed amendment thereto be postponed for further consideration. Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the motion?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: - As it is just about midnight, I think we might report progress. We have made good progress so far.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I would like to call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that tomorrow is the 30th of April, and that this is a long Bill and will take a lot of consistent, steady work before it is disposed of. I think if we put in another couple of hours' work to-night it is not too much to expect. We have had practically no late sittings during this session. I do not know what the feeling of the other members is, but I would like to get through the business of the session sometime, and particularly to get through this Bill. To ask the House to sit occasionally until two o'clock in the morning is not unreasonable. In past years it was a common thing to sit until one or two o'clock every morning.
Some of us were younger then.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: All of us.
I agree with the minister and think we should sit until two o'clock. The Opposition has done nothing but try to delay business the whole evening.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman apparently will not have to attend a committee meeting to-morrow morning. I have to attend a committee on a very important Bill, the Indian Bill; it is my duty to be there; and I want to be here for the discussion on this Bill also. It is unfair to ask me to sit here after twelve o'clock when I have to attend a com-

mittee of this House to-morrow morning at ten o'clock.
Why don't you go home and go to bed?
If I were doing as little as the hon. gentleman I could go home and remain home until the end of the session, and the business of the country would proceed just as well.

We had better come to an understanding on this question and not fill the air with fire. My hon. friend fom Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is absolutely right; to-morrow morning we have to attend important committee meetings. I realize that the ministers have to attend at their offices, but others who help to do the work of this House, like my hon. friend from Quebec East, have also to attend meetings of special committees, and we cannot do so if we sit here until two o'clock in the morning. The hon. member for Car-leton (Mr. Boyce) may be quite willing to sit into the early hours of the morning when he attends to the business of the House so seldom, but he cannot measure others by his own yardstick. I think midnight is a fair hour, but if we are called upon to sit beyond midnight we will sit.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In our younger days we used to think midnight was too early to rise.
We are older now.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose in face of the statement of my hon. friend from Three Rivers II may take it for granted that we are not going to make any further progress.
I am sure you will not.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: 1 do think we will have to sit a little later during the balance of the session.
Then do it at the beginning of the week when we are not "all in."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The session has been one of very early adjournments-perhaps it has made a record in that respect. In my long experience in this House I have known no other session when we have risen so early. But while I see the situation to-night, I do think that next week when we take up this amendment we ought to sit a little steadier and later if we hope to reach a final determination within a treasonable time. I agree that reasonable opportunity should be given for discussion, and personally I would like to sit a couple

of hours more to-night. However, under the circumstances, as apparently we will not advance matters any further, I move that the committee do now rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. 1
must remind the hon. members that there is a well known rule of the House which provides that when the House adjourns the members must keep their seats until the Speaker has left the Chair. It also provides that when the Speaker is putting a question no hon. member shall walk out of or across the House or make any noise or disturbance. Let me assure hon. gentlemen that these remarks are not dictated by any desire on the part of the Speaker to exalt his own position hut by an earnest desire to maintain the traditional dignity and decorum olf the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The member for
Carleton (iMr. Boyce) is leaving the Chamber.

Out of respect to the Speaker I will take my seat, hut not out of respect to hon. gentlemen opposite.
On motion of Sir Henry Drayton the House adjourned at twelve o'clock (midnight).
Friday, April 30, 1920.
